articles.title: Fix Go Goroutine Leaks & Scale ClickHouse Monoliths
articles.excerpt: 💡 Originally published on Bijak Technology Enterprise Journal with full interactive parameter benchmarks. At 02:30 AM, production metrics on our modular monolith system suddenly spiked. The memory co…
articles.body: 💡 Originally published on Bijak Technology Enterprise Journal with full interactive parameter benchmarks. At 02:30 AM, production metrics on our modular monolith system suddenly spiked. The memory consumption graph in our monitoring dashboard showed an unrelenting upward linear curve, culminating in pod crashes driven by the Out-Of-Memory (OOM) Killer. The root cause was not a traditional heap memory leak, but rather the accumulation of thousands of hanging Go goroutines caused by unhandled context cancellation within analytical background workers processing millions of daily telemetry rows. At the enterprise level, when telemetry data volume hits hundreds of millions of rows per day, row-oriented storage architectures like PostgreSQL hit severe physical bottlenecks.

articles.title: On Error Resume Next, PLEASE
articles.excerpt: Over the past several articles, we've explored the stranger corners of PHP, JavaScript, Python, C#, Java, and, of course, Perl. Especially Perl. We've encountered variables that lie, loops that corrup…
articles.body: Over the past several articles, we've explored the stranger corners of PHP, JavaScript, Python, C#, Java, and, of course, Perl. Especially Perl. We've encountered variables that lie, loops that corrupt data, compilers that enthusiastically approve terrible decisions, and programming languages that seem to regard predictability as an optional feature. But there's a problem. We've barely scratched the surface of programming-language insanity. The history of software development is littered with languages that introduced ideas so peculiar they deserve to be preserved in a museum. Some were brilliant. Some were genuinely useful. Some were products of their era. And a few appear to have been designed by people who were actively trying to make programmers suffer.
articles.author: Jean-Luc Martel

articles.excerpt: Every hackathon, meetup and conference has the same invisible failure. Somewhere in the room there is a developer who needs someone who understands customers, and a business student who needs someone…
articles.body: Every hackathon, meetup and conference has the same invisible failure. Somewhere in the room there is a developer who needs someone who understands customers, and a business student who needs someone who can build. They are ten metres apart. They never speak. They leave with the people they arrived with. At Hacktoberfest 2026 Hack Day Kampala × MUBS , a team of seven people from five universities decided to build for exactly that failure. We called it Matchpiece : find your missing piece. Out of 8 projects and 67 participants, it won 1st place in the Best Open-Source AI Project challenge , and the team was forwarded to the MUBS EIIC incubator. This post is about the one idea behind it, because I think it applies far beyond hackathons.

articles.title: The Receiver Should Refuse the Second Copy — Your Retry Loop Never Will.
articles.excerpt: Yesterday's fix was on the sending side. A slow receiver took 2.5 seconds to answer, the sweeper checked every second, heard silence, and sent the same order three times. The fix was a claim row: one…
articles.body: Yesterday's fix was on the sending side. A slow receiver took 2.5 seconds to answer, the sweeper checked every second, heard silence, and sent the same order three times. The fix was a claim row: one row per delivery key, claimed once, so the second and third ticks had nothing to send. Three deliveries became one. Then itsvicmoreno asked the question that undoes that fix, politely, in the comments. What if the acknowledgement is lost AFTER the write? The receiver has already taken the order, already charged the card, already sent the email. The sender never hears back, decides the delivery failed, and sends it again. The claim row cannot help you there. The sender did its job, the row says done or it says nothing useful, and a second copy is already on its way.

articles.body: “Nightmare at 20,000 Feet” is one of the all-time great episodes of The Twilight Zone . Starring William Shatner, the story is about a man who is taking his first flight after having had a nervous breakdown. During the flight, he looks out the window and sees a creature, called a gremlin, on the wing that taunts him and tears apart pieces of the plane. No one can see the gremlin but him, and even his own wife attributes it to his fragile mental state. The story is a brilliant commentary on paranoia and Shatner was captivating in the role. It was so good that it sometimes overshadows Shatner’s other great episode of The Twilight Zone , which premiered 66 years ago today.

ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers.

articles.title: NASA Launches Nuclear Power Systems Student Contest
articles.excerpt: NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the Un…
articles.body: The thematics for the 2026-2027 Radioisotope Power Systems Power to Explore Student Challenge Credit: NASA / David Lam NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision. Students are also invited to write a short essay about a “superpower” of their own. Submissions are due March 1, 2027. Every mission requires a power source. Some of the most interesting locations to study on our Moon face some of the harshest conditions.

articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
articles.excerpt: Voyager 1 just reached a light-day in space, but Voyager 2 won't do the same until 2035, due to speed choices made throughout their 50-year missions.
articles.body: Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer?

articles.body: 2 min read NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records Two NASA Space Apps Challenge participants in Vilhena, Brazil work together during the annual hackathon on their project submission. NASA On Nov. 14 and 15, NASA held the annual Space Apps Challenge with a record-breaking 181,835 registered participants taking part in 593 events around the world. The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. This year, the hackathon drew 59% more registrants and was the 5th year in a row with increased participation. Since 2012, NASA Space Apps Challenge has hosted the two-day event, which has included more than 600,000 people from more than 190 countries.

articles.title: Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?
articles.excerpt: The British company Foundational thinks its laser-reflecting tech can help humanity fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.
articles.body: A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors.
